differences.description: Base array index offset

schema_requirements: Table must include an array-typed column: PG uses INTEGER[] or TEXT[], MySQL uses a JSON type column to store arrays, Oracle uses VARRAY or nested table
data_requirements: Each array must contain at least 3 elements to distinguish the difference between 0-based and 1-based indexing. For example, PG needs to insert ARRAY[10, 20, 30], MySQL needs to insert JSON_ARRAY(10, 20, 30), Oracle needs to insert num_array(10, 20, 30)
query_requirements: Queries must use array subscript access syntax (arr[N])
Both subscript 0 and subscript 1 must be tested to expose the index offset differences among the three databases
data_anti_patterns: Avoid using single-element arrays, otherwise the difference in starting index values cannot be demonstrated
key_traps: PostgreSQL uses 1-based arrays (arr[1] is the first element), while MySQL and Oracle use 0-based arrays (arr[0] is the first element)
When migrating across dialects, all array subscript references must be adjusted by ±1 to match the target database's indexing rules

differences.description: NULL value sorting behavior

schema_requirements: Table must contain at least one sortable column (such as VARCHAR, INTEGER, or DATE) to demonstrate the difference in NULL value sorting position
data_requirements: Data must contain NULL values and several non-NULL values to compare sorting results in ORDER BY
Non-NULL values should be distributed on both sides of the logical position where NULL may appear (e.g., 1, 2, 3 and NULL)
query_patterns: SELECT col FROM t ORDER BY col ASC;
SELECT col FROM t ORDER BY col DESC;
query_requirements: Queries must use an ORDER BY clause to sort a column containing NULLs in ascending or descending order
MySQL treats NULL as the smallest value and sorts it first by default, while PostgreSQL and Oracle treat NULL as the largest value and sort it last by default
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having all rows in the table have NULL or non-NULL values in this column, otherwise the relative sorting difference between NULL and other values cannot be demonstrated
Avoid using conditions like IS NULL that filter out NULL values
key_traps: When migrating across dialects, if the sorting behavior needs to remain consistent, explicit NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST must be specified in the ORDER BY clause
MySQL's default behavior is the opposite of PG/Oracle; direct migration may cause the sorted result order to be reversed

differences.description: Whether division is type-sensitive (integer division vs floating-point division)

schema_requirements: Table must contain at least two integer-typed columns (INT or BIGINT) for division operations
data_requirements: Data must include rows where the dividend is not evenly divisible by the divisor (e.g., 5 and 2) to expose the truncation difference in integer division
It should also include rows that are evenly divisible as a control (e.g., 4 and 2)
query_patterns: SELECT CAST(int_col_a AS FLOAT) / int_col_b FROM t;
query_requirements: Queries must use two integer columns for division operations
PostgreSQL enables TYPED_DIVISION by default; integer division returns INTEGER (fractional part truncated), while MySQL/Oracle return DECIMAL/NUMBER (fractional part preserved)
Tests need to compare division results without explicit type conversion
data_anti_patterns: Avoid making all dividends evenly divisible by the divisor, otherwise all three databases yield the same result and no difference is shown
Avoid defining columns as FLOAT/DOUBLE type, otherwise integer division behavior will not be triggered
key_traps: In PostgreSQL PG 10+ versions, integer division returns an integer by default (truncated), while MySQL and Oracle always return a result with a fractional part
When migrating across dialects, if fractional precision is relied upon, operands must be explicitly cast to NUMERIC or FLOAT in PostgreSQL

differences.description: Whether division by zero returns NULL instead of raising an error

schema_requirements: Table must contain two numeric columns (INT, BIGINT, or DECIMAL) serving as dividend and divisor respectively
data_requirements: Data must include at least one row where the divisor is 0
It should also contain normal records with non-zero divisors as a control
query_patterns: SELECT a / b FROM (SELECT 10 AS a, 0 AS b UNION ALL SELECT 5 AS a, 2 AS b) AS t;
query_requirements: Queries must use the division operator (/) and the operands must include a divisor that can be 0
MySQL needs SAFE_DIVISION mode enabled (enabled by default) to return NULL, while PG and Oracle throw an exception by default
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having all divisors non-zero, otherwise the difference between exceptions and silent handling cannot be triggered
Avoid using NULL instead of 0 as divisor, because operations with NULL usually return NULL and do not reflect division-by-zero behavior differences
key_traps: MySQL returns NULL when dividing by 0 when SAFE_DIVISION=ON, while PostgreSQL and Oracle directly throw a 'division by zero' error
When migrating across dialects, MySQL code will fail in PG/Oracle; explicit CASE WHEN divisor != 0 THEN ... ELSE NULL END protection logic must be added

differences.description: Whether NULL becomes an empty string in CONCAT

schema_requirements: Table must contain string-typed columns (VARCHAR or TEXT) to test the CONCAT function
Table must contain at least one string column that allows NULL
data_requirements: Data must include rows with NULL values to observe the difference in how CONCAT handles NULL
Data should also contain non-NULL values as a control to verify normal concatenation behavior
query_patterns: SELECT CONCAT(col1, 'suffix') FROM t WHERE col1 IS NULL;
query_requirements: Queries must use the CONCAT function for string concatenation
In PG, CONCAT treats NULL as an empty string and returns a result; in MySQL and Oracle, CONCAT returns NULL when encountering NULL
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having all columns involved in CONCAT non-NULL, otherwise the differences in NULL handling among the three databases cannot be demonstrated
key_traps: The CONCAT function in PostgreSQL has the behavior: as long as one argument is NULL, concatenation continues (NULL treated as empty string), while MySQL and Oracle CONCAT directly returns NULL when encountering NULL
When migrating across dialects, if the target database does not support this behavior (e.g., MySQL/Oracle), each argument should be wrapped with COALESCE to emulate PG behavior

differences.description: Whether the || operator is string concatenation

data_requirements: At least two string-typed constants or variables need to be included for concatenation testing
query_requirements: Queries must use the double pipe || operator for string concatenation
MySQL needs to be translated to CONCAT() function; PG and Oracle retain the || syntax
data_anti_patterns: Avoid directly concatenating numeric-typed columns; although some dialects implicitly convert, it may hide the differences
key_traps: In MySQL, || is a logical OR operator (depending on SQL_MODE settings), not a string concatenation operator
In PG and Oracle, || defaults to string concatenation and requires no special configuration
When migrating across dialects, MySQL must explicitly switch to the CONCAT() function

differences.description: Identifier case normalization strategy

schema_requirements: Table must contain identifiers with mixed case (e.g., column names or table names containing both uppercase and lowercase letters)
query_requirements: Queries must use double-quoted identifiers to preserve the original case
MySQL uses the CASE_SENSITIVE strategy, distinguishes case, and must match exactly
PostgreSQL uses the LOWERCASE strategy, automatically converting to lowercase, and is case-insensitive
Oracle uses the UPPERCASE strategy, automatically converting to uppercase, and is case-insensitive
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having all identifiers be entirely lowercase or entirely uppercase, otherwise the normalization difference cannot be demonstrated

Avoid using unquoted identifiers, because the three databases handle unquoted identifiers differently (usually converting to uppercase or lowercase), which makes it impossible to test the NORMALIZATION_STRATEGY attribute
key_traps: MySQL is case-sensitive by default (depending on the file system), but at the SQL parser level, double quotes must be explicitly used and it relies on configuration
PG and Oracle automatically convert identifier case during parsing, causing names inside double quotes to behave differently across dialects
When migrating across dialects, if the source database uses double quotes with mixed case, the target database may not find the corresponding object due to different normalization strategies

differences.description: Whether user-defined types are supported

schema_requirements: Table must include a user-defined type column (e.g., PG's ENUM/composite types, Oracle's OBJECT/VARRAY)
data_requirements: Data must contain legal values that conform to the custom type definition
Avoid inserting values that do not conform to custom type constraints, which would cause syntax errors
query_requirements: Queries must reference an already-defined user-defined type column
MySQL cannot execute queries involving user-defined types; they must be translated to native types or the logic must be removed
PG and Oracle support direct use of the type, but the specific type definition syntax differs
data_anti_patterns: Avoid attempting to execute queries that depend on this feature in dialects that do not support custom types (e.g., MySQL)
key_traps: MySQL does not support user-defined type definitions such as CREATE TYPE at all; related functionality must be simulated with ENUM or JSON
PG supports rich UDTs (enums, domains, composite types), and Oracle supports object types and nested tables
When migrating across dialects, if the original SQL relies on UDT features, it must be rewritten as native type logic in MySQL

differences.description: Whether TABLESAMPLE size is a percentage

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain enough data rows (at least 1000 rows is recommended) so that percentage sampling can produce a visible difference in sample size.
data_requirements: No special data values are required; ordinary data is sufficient to trigger the sampling logic.
The data distribution should be uniform to avoid extreme skewness causing unpredictable sampling results.
query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (5 PERCENT);
query_requirements: When using TABLESAMPLE in MySQL, the number of rows must be explicitly specified, or no PERCENT keyword should be used (row count is the default).
In PostgreSQL and Oracle, if a number is specified in TABLESAMPLE, it defaults to a percentage (e.g., TABLESAMPLE 10 means 10%).
Small percentage values must also be tested to verify whether the returned row count ratios are consistent across the three databases.
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having too few rows in the table (e.g., fewer than 10 rows); otherwise the difference between percentage and row count is not obvious and the semantic difference cannot be demonstrated.
Avoid leaving randomness unfixed when using the REPEATABLE seed parameter, as result fluctuations may mask the differences.
key_traps: MySQL's TABLESAMPLE syntax does not support percentage semantics; it must be converted to LIMIT or an approximate row count calculation.
PG and Oracle interpret TABLESAMPLE as a percentage by default, while MySQL interprets it as a row count; cross-dialect translation must convert units.
Oracle's SYSTEM/BERNOULLI clause behaves slightly differently from PG's SYSTEM/BERNOULLI; version compatibility should be noted.

differences.description: Whether identifiers can start with a digit

query_requirements: Queries need to use identifiers starting with a digit as column names or aliases.
MySQL allows identifiers starting with a digit (e.g., SELECT 123abc), while PG and Oracle will raise an error.
key_traps: MySQL allows identifiers to start with a digit, but PG and Oracle strictly require identifiers to start with a letter or underscore.
When converting across dialects, all identifiers starting with a digit must be enclosed in double quotes ("123col") or escaped with escape characters.

differences.description: Whether the table alias comes after TABLESAMPLE

query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (10) AS alias;
SELECT * FROM t AS alias TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (10);
query_requirements: Queries need to use the TABLESAMPLE clause together with a table alias.
Oracle allows the alias after TABLESAMPLE, while MySQL and PostgreSQL require the alias to be before TABLESAMPLE.
key_traps: Oracle syntax is: FROM table_name SAMPLE ... AS alias
MySQL and PostgreSQL syntax is: FROM table_name AS alias SAMPLE ...
When converting across dialects, the alias position must be adjusted; otherwise a syntax error will occur.

differences.description: Whether locking reads (SELECT...FOR UPDATE) are supported

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain at least one column for data queries, and the table should be locked by another transaction to trigger row-level lock differences.
data_requirements: The table must contain data rows that can be locked by SELECT...FOR UPDATE.
The test environment must support multi-transaction concurrency scenarios (e.g., opening two sessions).
query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT * FROM t WHERE status = 'pending' FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
query_requirements: Queries must use the FOR UPDATE clause to attempt to acquire row-level locks.
Oracle explicitly supports LOCKING_READS_SUPPORTED; MySQL/PostgreSQL support must be verified through specific syntax.
data_anti_patterns: Avoid executing on read-only databases or storage engines without transaction support (e.g., MyISAM).
Avoid executing FOR UPDATE on an empty result set, as the locking behavior cannot be demonstrated.
key_traps: Oracle explicitly declares support for the LOCKING_READS_SUPPORTED property, while MySQL and PostgreSQL depend on specific syntax implementations.
The semantics of FOR UPDATE may differ between dialects (e.g., Oracle's FOR UPDATE NOWAIT versus MySQL's default blocking behavior).

differences.description: Whether to promote to an inferred datetime type

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain date/time related columns (DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP, or VARCHAR for storing date strings).
data_requirements: Data should contain non-standard or mixed-type date values to trigger differences in type inference behavior.
It should contain specific data patterns that may be considered 'inferred datetime types' (e.g., scenarios in MySQL where certain strings are automatically converted to DATETIME).
query_patterns: SELECT CAST(date_str AS DATETIME) FROM t;
SELECT date_col + INTERVAL '1 day' FROM t;
query_requirements: Queries need to use expressions involving date/time type conversions or operations.
It is necessary to test the behavioral differences between MySQL with PROMOTE_TO_INFERRED_DATETIME_TYPE enabled and PG/Oracle.
Compare the data type or precision differences returned by the three databases for the same date operation.
data_anti_patterns: Avoid using standard, explicitly declared DATETIME columns; otherwise the differences in inference behavior cannot be demonstrated.
Avoid having all date values in exactly the same format, as this makes it difficult to expose differences in type inference logic.
key_traps: MySQL's PROMOTE_TO_INFERRED_DATETIME_TYPE property affects implicit type conversion behavior, while PG/Oracle strictly follow explicit declarations.
When migrating across dialects, check implicit conversion logic that relies on this property to prevent runtime type errors.

differences.description: Whether a table can be referenced as a column

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain a VARCHAR or TEXT column used to store column names (e.g., col_name).
The table needs to contain a numeric or string column used to store values (e.g., value_col).
data_requirements: Data must be inserted into the main table, where the value of the column name column corresponds to the name of another existing table.
The referenced table must exist and contain at least one row of data.
A specific scenario must be constructed: a column value in the main table equals the name of the target table.
query_patterns: SELECT t1.col_name, (SELECT value_col FROM t1.col_name LIMIT 1) FROM t1;
SELECT t1.col_name, (SELECT * FROM t1.col_name WHERE rownum = 1) FROM t1;
query_requirements: Queries need to use dynamic table name reference syntax, i.e., the FROM clause in parentheses directly uses the column value as the table name.
PostgreSQL supports directly parsing the column value as a table name for correlated queries.
MySQL and Oracle do not support this syntax; it must be implemented using dynamic SQL or JOIN instead.
data_anti_patterns: Avoid illegal table names in the column name column (e.g., names containing special characters, spaces, or reserved words).
Avoid referencing non-existent tables; otherwise the query will fail rather than demonstrate the syntax difference.
key_traps: PostgreSQL allows using a variable/column name as a table name in the FROM clause (TABLES_REFERENCEABLE_AS_COLUMNS=True).
MySQL and Oracle strictly prohibit using a column name directly as a table name in the FROM clause; it will cause a syntax error.
When converting across dialects, such PostgreSQL syntax must be rewritten as dynamic SQL or an explicit JOIN in MySQL/Oracle.

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: CHARSET

query_requirements: The query must use the MySQL-specific CHARSET keyword as a function call to get the charset of a string or column.
PG and Oracle do not support this syntax; it needs to be translated to return NULL or raise an exception.
key_traps: CHARSET is a MySQL-specific keyword/function used to get the charset name.
PG and Oracle have no corresponding built-in function; executing it directly will cause a syntax error.

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: DISTINCTROW

query_patterns: SELECT DISTINCTROW col1, col2 FROM t;
SELECT DISTINCTROW * FROM t WHERE condition = 1;
query_requirements: The query needs to use the DISTINCTROW keyword instead of the standard DISTINCT.
MySQL supports DISTINCTROW; PG and Oracle do not support this syntax, so it needs to be translated to DISTINCT.
key_traps: DISTINCTROW is a MySQL-specific keyword, functionally equivalent to DISTINCT (ignoring duplicate rows).
Neither PostgreSQL nor Oracle supports DISTINCTROW; it must be replaced with DISTINCT when converting across dialects.

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: FORCE

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain a numeric column (e.g., INT) to test the effect of forcing an index.
data_requirements: Data should contain multiple rows so that differences in the query execution plan can be observed.
Data distribution should have selectivity differences so that the FORCE hint has an actual impact.
query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t USE INDEX (idx_col) FORCE WHERE col = 10;
SELECT * FROM t FORCE INDEX (idx_col) WHERE col > 5;
query_requirements: The query must contain the MySQL-specific FORCE keyword to modify the index hint.
PG and Oracle do not support this syntax; FORCE must be removed or replaced with other optimizer hint mechanisms.
In MySQL, FORCE can be used alone or combined with INDEX/INDEX_HINT.
data_anti_patterns: Avoid single-row data, as it cannot reflect differences in index selection strategy.
Avoid having all column values identical, leaving the optimizer no choice.
key_traps: FORCE is a MySQL-specific index hint modifier; PG and Oracle do not support this syntax at all.
When migrating to PG, the FORCE keyword must be removed; you may need to use hint comments or adjust statistics.
Oracle uses hints such as /*+ INDEX(t idx_col) */, which is completely different from MySQL FORCE syntax.

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: IGNORE

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain a numeric column (INT or DECIMAL) to demonstrate division operations.
The table needs to contain a column with a unique or primary key constraint to trigger IGNORE behavior.
data_requirements: Data needs to contain duplicate values to trigger unique constraint conflicts during INSERT.
Data should include rows that insert normally and rows that will cause conflicts.
query_patterns: INSERT IGNORE INTO t (id, val) VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b');
INSERT IGNORE INTO t (id, val) SELECT id, val FROM source_table;
query_requirements: The query needs to use the INSERT IGNORE syntax.
When the target table has a unique constraint and the inserted data conflicts, MySQL silently ignores the error and continues execution.
PG/Oracle do not support the IGNORE keyword; it needs to be translated to use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (PG) or a MERGE statement to handle conflicts.
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having all inserted data not violate the unique constraint, otherwise the effect of IGNORE cannot be demonstrated.
Avoid not defining a unique index or primary key, because IGNORE is only meaningful when a conflict occurs.
key_traps: MySQL's INSERT IGNORE does not report an error or roll back a single row when a unique key conflict occurs; it skips that row.
PostgreSQL needs to use the ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING clause to achieve the same effect.
Oracle needs to use a MERGE statement with a NOT MATCHED condition or PL/SQL exception handling to simulate IGNORE behavior.

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: KEY

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain a column that is defined as a KEY in MySQL (such as UNIQUE KEY or PRIMARY KEY).
query_patterns: CREATE TABLE t (id INT, name VARCHAR(50), UNIQUE KEY idx_name (name));
query_requirements: The query needs to use the CREATE TABLE statement to define constraints.
MySQL uses the KEY keyword to define a unique index or primary key; PG and Oracle do not support this syntax.
key_traps: MySQL allows KEY as shorthand for UNIQUE KEY or PRIMARY KEY; PG and Oracle must use UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY respectively.
When converting across dialects, KEY must be replaced with the standard constraint keyword of the target dialect.

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: LOCK TABLES

query_patterns: LOCK TABLES t1 READ, t2 WRITE;
LOCK TABLES t1 IN SHARE MODE;
query_requirements: The query must use MySQL's specific LOCK TABLES syntax for explicit table locking.
This statement cannot be executed in PostgreSQL or Oracle; it needs to be converted to the corresponding row-level locking or transaction isolation mechanism.
key_traps: MySQL's LOCK TABLES is a DDL/DCL hybrid statement used to explicitly lock an entire table.
PostgreSQL does not support the LOCK TABLES keyword; it usually implements row-level locking via SELECT ... FOR UPDATE/SHARE, or uses SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL for control.
Oracle also does not support LOCK TABLES; you need to use ALTER TABLE ... LOCK or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: MEMBER OF

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain an array-type column (such as PostgreSQL's INTEGER[] or TEXT[]) for MEMBER OF operations.
Or the table needs to contain a JSON/JSONB type column (MySQL 8.0+ supports JSON, PG supports JSONB).
data_requirements: Data needs to include array or JSON array values, e.g., [1,2,3] or {"key": "value"}.
Test rows need to include the value to be matched (such as number 2 or string 'test') and control rows that do not contain that value.
query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t WHERE value_col MEMBER OF (1, 2, 3);
SELECT * FROM t WHERE json_col MEMBER OF '[1, 2, 3]'::jsonb;
query_requirements: The query needs to use the MEMBER OF keyword for membership determination.
The right-side argument must be a constant list, subquery, or array literal.
PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support this syntax; it needs to be translated to = ANY(ARRAY[]) or IN with UNNEST.
data_anti_patterns: Avoid an empty array or NULL value as the right-side argument, as it may produce unexpected results or syntax errors.
Avoid data type mismatches (e.g., comparing an integer array with a string), which can cause the logic to fail.
key_traps: MySQL's MEMBER OF is a syntax keyword; PG/Oracle do not have this feature and it must be rewritten as equivalent logic.
In PG, use = ANY(ARRAY[...]) or EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM UNNEST(...) AS x WHERE x = col).
In Oracle, use IN with collection functions or use XMLTable to parse JSON arrays.

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: MOD

query_requirements: The query needs to use the MOD keyword as a modulo operator or function.
In MySQL, MOD can be used both as a binary operator (a MOD b) and as a function (MOD(a,b)); PG and Oracle do not support this syntax.
key_traps: MySQL supports the MOD keyword for modulo operations; neither PostgreSQL nor Oracle supports this keyword.
In PG and Oracle, MOD must be replaced with the % symbol (e.g., a % b) or the mod() function (Oracle) / remainder() (PG).
Note that MySQL's MOD is a reserved word; when used directly as an identifier it needs backticks, while PG/Oracle do not have this restriction but can use other syntax as alternatives.

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: SEPARATOR

query_patterns: SELECT CONCAT_WS(',', col1, col2) FROM t;
query_requirements: The query requires using the SEPARATOR keyword as a parameter of the CONCAT function
In MySQL, 'STR1', 'STR2' SEPARATOR ',' is valid syntax; PG and Oracle do not support this syntax
key_traps: MySQL's SEPARATOR is used in the CONCAT function to specify a delimiter; PG/Oracle do not have this keyword
When converting across dialects, 'STR1', 'STR2' SEPARATOR ',' must be rewritten as CONCAT_WS or string concatenation

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: SIGNED

query_requirements: The query requires using MySQL-specific CAST(... AS SIGNED) syntax to convert a number or string to a signed integer
PG and Oracle do not support the SIGNED keyword; it must be translated to CAST(... AS INTEGER) or CAST(... AS INT)
key_traps: MySQL's SIGNED is a type modifier used to explicitly specify a signed integer type (equivalent to INT)
PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support the SIGNED keyword in CAST syntax; INTEGER, INT, or NUMBER must be used

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: SIGNED INTEGER

query_patterns: SELECT CAST(x AS SIGNED) FROM t;
query_requirements: The query requires using MySQL-specific SIGNED or SIGNED INTEGER type conversion syntax
PG and Oracle do not support this keyword; it must be translated to CAST(... AS INTEGER) or TO_NUMBER()
key_traps: MySQL's SIGNED is an alias equivalent to SIGNED INTEGER or BIGINT (depending on the context)
PG uses ::INTEGER or CAST(... AS INTEGER); Oracle uses TO_NUMBER() or CAST(... AS NUMBER)
Directly porting SIGNED to PG/Oracle will cause parsing errors

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: SOUNDS LIKE

query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t WHERE name SOUNDS LIKE 'John';
SELECT name, description FROM products WHERE product_name SOUNDS LIKE 'Smith' OR category SOUNDS LIKE 'Carpentry';
query_requirements: The query requires using MySQL-exclusive SOUNDS LIKE keyword for fuzzy matching
PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support this syntax; it must be translated to a phonetic algorithm implementation (e.g., PG's soundex function or Oracle's utl_match)
data_anti_patterns: Avoid using fully exact-match strings; otherwise the sound-similarity-based feature of SOUNDS LIKE cannot be demonstrated
key_traps: SOUNDS LIKE is a MySQL-specific implementation of the Soundex algorithm; PG and Oracle do not natively support this keyword

When converting across dialects, SOUNDS LIKE must be replaced with the corresponding database's phonetic functions (e.g., PG: soundex(col) = soundex('value'), Oracle: utl_match.edit_distance_soundex, etc.)

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: UNLOCK TABLES

query_requirements: The query must use the MySQL-specific UNLOCK TABLES statement
This statement is used to release tables locked by LOCK TABLES; PG and Oracle do not support this syntax
key_traps: UNLOCK TABLES is a MySQL transaction-control-related statement mixing DML/DDL; PG and Oracle have no corresponding keyword
When migrating across dialects, if the original SQL contains UNLOCK TABLES, it must be removed or replaced with the corresponding row-level lock release mechanism (e.g., explicit COMMIT) in PG/Oracle

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: UNSIGNED

schema_requirements: The table must contain an integer-type column (INT, BIGINT, etc.), and that column must be explicitly declared with the UNSIGNED attribute in its definition
data_requirements: The data must include negative numbers to trigger behavioral differences between MySQL and PG/Oracle when handling unsigned numbers
Alternatively, the data must include positive numbers greater than the signed integer maximum (e.g., values outside the BIGINT range) to test overflow handling differences
query_patterns: SELECT CAST(-1 AS UNSIGNED) FROM t;
SELECT CAST(4294967295 AS UNSIGNED) FROM t;
query_requirements: The query requires using the CAST function to convert a value to the UNSIGNED type
MySQL supports the UNSIGNED keyword, while PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support it, causing syntax errors
In PG, UNSIGNED must be removed or simulated with other mechanisms (such as CHECK constraints); in Oracle, NUMBER must be used along with constraints
data_anti_patterns: Avoid inserting only non-negative numbers within the signed integer range; otherwise the semantic differences introduced by UNSIGNED cannot be demonstrated
key_traps: MySQL's UNSIGNED is a data type modifier that restricts the numeric range from 0 to the maximum value
PG and Oracle do not have the UNSIGNED concept; direct translation will cause an error, so the keyword or conversion logic must be removed
When migrating across dialects, note the difference in numeric overflow behavior: MySQL allows storing large positive numbers, while PG/Oracle are signed by default

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: UNSIGNED INTEGER

schema_requirements: The table must contain a column of unsigned integer type (UNSIGNED INT or UNSIGNED BIGINT)
query_patterns: SELECT CAST('3000000000' AS UNSIGNED) FROM DUAL;
query_requirements: The query requires using the MySQL-specific UNSIGNED type modifier
PG and Oracle do not support the UNSIGNED keyword; it must be translated to plain INTEGER/BIGINT with overflow handling logic
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having all data within the signed integer range (-2147483648 to 2147483647); otherwise the UNSIGNED characteristic differences cannot be demonstrated
key_traps: MySQL's UNSIGNED is part of the type definition; PG/Oracle do not have this keyword
When converting across dialects, MySQL's UNSIGNED columns are usually mapped to signed types of the same bit width in PG/Oracle, but additional checks are needed for data exceeding the positive range

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: YEAR

query_requirements: The query requires using the YEAR function as a scalar function call (not as a column name or table name)
PG and Oracle do not support the YEAR keyword; it must be translated to EXTRACT(YEAR FROM date_col) or TO_CHAR(date_col, 'YYYY')
data_anti_patterns: Avoid using YEAR as a column alias or identifier; it is legal in MySQL but may cause reserved-word conflicts in PG/Oracle
key_traps: MySQL's YEAR is a function that can directly extract the year from a date expression
PG uses EXTRACT(YEAR FROM expr); Oracle uses EXTRACT(YEAR FROM expr) or TO_CHAR(expr, 'YYYY')
Directly porting the YEAR() function will cause PG/Oracle syntax errors

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: _ARMSCII8

query_requirements: Query needs to use MySQL-specific _ARMSCII8 character set prefix syntax or CONVERT function to specify ARMScii8 encoding
PG and Oracle do not support this syntax; it needs to be translated to the corresponding encoding conversion function (e.g., PG's encode/decode or Oracle's RAWTOHEX, etc.)
key_traps: MySQL uses the _ARMSCII8'string' syntax to directly specify the string encoding; PG/Oracle do not have this prefix syntax
When converting across dialects, the ARMSCII8 encoding needs to be converted to an encoding supported by the target database, or handled using binary processing

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: _ASCII

query_requirements: The query needs to use MySQL-specific _ASCII prefix syntax to convert string literals to ASCII code values
This syntax cannot be executed directly in PostgreSQL and Oracle; it needs to be translated to the corresponding character encoding function
key_traps: _ASCII is a MySQL-specific string literal modifier; PG and Oracle do not support this syntax
When translating to PG, use the ASCII() function instead (e.g., SELECT ASCII('A')); Oracle needs to use ASCII() or a combination of CHR/CONVERT

differences.description: MySQL-specific keyword: _BIG5

query_requirements: The query needs to use MySQL-specific character set prefix syntax _BIG5'string'
PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support this syntax; it needs to be translated to the corresponding encoding conversion function or the prefix removed
key_traps: _BIG5 is a MySQL-specific string literal prefix used to specify BIG5 encoding
PG and Oracle cannot parse the _BIG5 prefix; direct execution will raise a syntax error

MySQL must use backticks (`); PostgreSQL and Oracle must use double quotes (").

In MySQL, single quotes are used for strings, and double quotes may also be processed as strings in certain modes (depending on sql_mode); in PG/Oracle double quotes are strictly used for identifiers.
When copying MySQL SQL directly to PG/Oracle, backticks cause syntax errors and must be replaced with double quotes.

differences.description: Comment syntax

PG and Oracle test cases must not use # as a comment symbol.

At least one row with a nested JSON object is needed to test the extraction functionality
query_requirements: The query needs to use JSON extraction functions or operators
MySQL and PostgreSQL support using extraction syntax directly on JSON type columns; Oracle does not support the JSON_TYPE_REQUIRED_FOR_EXTRACTION feature
Oracle must use alternative approaches such as REGEXP_SUBSTR or XMLTABLE to handle JSON extraction
data_anti_patterns: Avoid storing plain text data that is not in JSON format, otherwise the JSON extraction difference cannot be triggered
Avoid empty or missing JSON structures, as NULL extraction results would mask the difference
key_traps: MySQL and PostgreSQL by default require the column type to be JSON/JSONB for efficient extraction; Oracle has no such mandatory requirement but needs different syntax
When converting across dialects, note that Oracle does not support direct JSON extraction operators, so the query logic needs to be restructured

differences.description: Whether JSON PATH supports bracketed keys

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain a JSON or JSONB type column for storing JSON data
data_requirements: The inserted JSON data must contain nested objects, and the key names need to use special characters (such as spaces, hyphens) or start with digits
For example: {"user name": "Alice", "1st-item": "value"}
query_requirements: The query needs to use standard JSON path operators (-> or ->>) to access keys containing non-identifier characters
MySQL does not support bracketed key syntax and requires simulating it with string concatenation or REGEXP_SUBSTR
PG and Oracle support this syntax and can directly parse key names with special characters
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having all key names be purely alphabetic with no special characters, otherwise the behavior is identical across all three databases and the difference cannot be shown
key_traps: MySQL's -> operator only supports simple key names; encountering spaces or special characters will cause an error or return NULL
PG and Oracle's -> operator supports bracketed key syntax and can correctly parse non-standard identifier key names
When converting across dialects, key names with special characters need to be wrapped in quotes or handled with other functions

differences.description: Whether the PAD function must specify a fill character

query_requirements: The query must use the PAD function (or padding functions such as LPAD/RPAD for left/right padding)
MySQL requires the PAD function to explicitly specify the third parameter (fill character), otherwise an error is raised
PG and Oracle's corresponding functions (LPAD/RPAD) allow omitting the fill character and default to a space
key_traps: MySQL's PAD() function signature enforces 3 parameters (string, length, fill character)
In PG and Oracle's LPAD/RPAD functions, the fill character is optional and defaults to a space
When converting across dialects, if the original SQL does not specify a fill character, the default value ' ' must be supplied for MySQL

differences.description: Whether derived values need to be wrapped in parentheses

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain at least one numeric or string column (such as INT, VARCHAR) for constructing derived subqueries
data_requirements: The data should contain multiple rows so that the derived subquery can produce aggregated or list results
Ensure the derived subquery returns a non-empty set to trigger the parenthesis wrapping logic
query_patterns: SELECT * FROM (SELECT col1, SUM(col2) as total FROM t GROUP BY col1) AS derived;
SELECT d.col1, d.total FROM (SELECT col1, SUM(col2) as total FROM t GROUP BY col1) AS d;
query_requirements: The query must include a derived subquery (a subquery used as part of the FROM clause)
PostgreSQL and Oracle wrap derived values in parentheses by default (WRAP_DERIVED_VALUES=True), while MySQL does not (False)
When translating, the parenthesis structure of the subquery should be adjusted according to the target dialect
data_anti_patterns: Avoid derived subqueries that return a single row without grouping, otherwise the parenthesis difference may not be visible
Avoid constant subqueries (such as SELECT 1); the query should depend on table column data to reflect structural differences
key_traps: In MySQL-generated SQL, derived subqueries have no parentheses, while PG/Oracle have parentheses; simply copying the SQL may cause syntax errors
When converting across dialects, the parenthesis generation behavior for derived subqueries must be explicitly controlled

differences.description: Whether DISTINCT supports multiple arguments

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain at least two numeric or string columns (such as col1, col2) for multi-argument DISTINCT testing
data_requirements: The data should contain multiple rows where the (col1, col2) combinations have duplicate values to verify the DISTINCT effect
Records with different column combinations but identical whole tuples need to be constructed, such as (1, 'A'), (1, 'A')
query_patterns: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT col1, col2) FROM t;
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT col1, col2) FILTER (WHERE col1 > 0) FROM t;
query_requirements: The query must use the multi-argument DISTINCT syntax COUNT(DISTINCT col1, col2)
MySQL and Oracle support this syntax; PostgreSQL does not and will raise a syntax error
In PostgreSQL, it must be translated to COUNT(DISTINCT CONCAT(col1, '|', col2)) or a subquery with deduplication
data_anti_patterns: Avoid making all (col1, col2) combinations in all rows unique, otherwise the multi-argument deduplication difference cannot be shown
Avoid columns containing NULL values, as the different NULL handling logic across the three databases would interfere with the results
key_traps: MySQL and Oracle allow COUNT(DISTINCT col1, col2), while PostgreSQL only supports single-argument DISTINCT
When converting across dialects, PostgreSQL must rewrite multi-argument DISTINCT as string concatenation or use a subquery to simulate deduplication

differences.description: Whether ARRAY ANY is supported

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain an array type column: PostgreSQL uses INTEGER[] or TEXT[], MySQL and Oracle use JSON or VARRAY
data_requirements: The data needs to contain non-empty array values (such as PG's ARRAY[1,2,3]) to perform ANY operations
Also need values that both match and do not match the array elements to verify the logic difference
query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t WHERE column = ANY(array_col);
SELECT * FROM t WHERE 'value' = ANY(SELECT array_col FROM t);
query_requirements: The query needs to use the ANY keyword together with an array column for condition evaluation
PostgreSQL supports this syntax directly; MySQL and Oracle do not, so it must be translated to an IN clause or a combination of UNNEST/EXISTS
data_anti_patterns: Avoid array columns being NULL, otherwise the ANY operation returns UNKNOWN or False in all three databases, failing to reflect the syntax support difference
Avoid empty arrays, as the ANY logic cannot be triggered
key_traps: PostgreSQL natively supports ARRAY ANY syntax, while MySQL and Oracle do not support this keyword at all
In MySQL, = ANY(...) must be converted to IN (...) or simulated with functions such as JSON_CONTAINS
In Oracle, use UNNEST (VARRAY) + IN, or EXISTS (SELECT ... FROM TABLE(array_col)) as alternatives

differences.description: Whether UNLOGGED TABLE is supported

schema_requirements: Table structures must include UNLOGGED TABLE definition syntax (e.g., CREATE TABLE t (...) WITHOUT OIDS or WITH (logging=false))
The database under test must support the structural capability of creating unlogged tables
query_patterns: CREATE TABLE test_unlogged (id INT) AS SELECT 1;
query_requirements: The query must use a DDL statement to attempt creating an unlogged table, validating the SUPPORTS_UNLOGGED_TABLES configuration attribute
PG should successfully create the unlogged table, while MySQL/Oracle should report an error or ignore this option
data_anti_patterns: Avoid using existing regular tables; the difference must be triggered by dynamically creating a table via DDL
key_traps: SUPPORTS_UNLOGGED_TABLES is a generator configuration attribute rather than pure SQL syntax; it should be validated in conjunction with an ORM or migration tool
MySQL and Oracle do not support the concept of unlogged tables; attempting to create one will raise a syntax error or be ignored
PG's unlogged tables are only for performance improvement; data is lost after a crash, so the test must consider data persistence expectations

differences.description: Whether the LIKE property is within the schema

schema_requirements: The table must include a column generated via the LIKE clause (e.g., CREATE TABLE t2 LIKE t1)
The table structure must support specifying generator attribute configuration in the CREATE TABLE statement
query_patterns: CREATE TABLE target_table (col1 INT) AS SELECT * FROM source_table;
query_requirements: The query must use CREATE TABLE ... LIKE syntax or AS SELECT syntax to create a new table
PostgreSQL's LIKE_PROPERTY_INSIDE_SCHEMA feature affects whether the generated column attributes retain the source table's defaults, constraints, etc.
MySQL and Oracle do not support this specific configuration option, and behavior may differ
key_traps: When PostgreSQL's LIKE syntax is processed within a schema, it may retain more source table attributes, while MySQL/Oracle may not retain them or may behave differently
When converting across dialects, verify whether the generated table structure fully retains the source table's constraints and defaults

differences.description: Whether the COPY statement has an INTO keyword

query_requirements: The query must use the COPY statement for data import or export
In MySQL and Oracle syntax, the COPY clause must include the INTO keyword (e.g., COPY INTO t), while PostgreSQL does not support the INTO keyword and directly uses COPY t FROM/TO
key_traps: MySQL and Oracle COPY statements are typically used for external table loading, and the syntax requires the INTO keyword to point to the target table
In PostgreSQL, the COPY statement specifies the table name directly after COPY; adding the INTO keyword is strictly prohibited and will cause an error
When converting across dialects, if translating from PG to MySQL/Oracle, INTO must be inserted; conversely, INTO must be removed when translating in the reverse direction

differences.description: Whether BETWEEN flags are supported

query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t WHERE col BETWEEN flags_col1 AND flags_col2;
query_requirements: The query must use a BETWEEN clause with bit-flag (flags) type columns for range evaluation
PG supports directly comparing bit-flag sets in BETWEEN, while MySQL and Oracle do not support this semantics or require special handling
data_anti_patterns: Avoid using regular numeric columns that are not bit-flag types; otherwise, the SUPPORTS_BETWEEN_FLAGS difference cannot be demonstrated
key_traps: PostgreSQL's SUPPORTS_BETWEEN_FLAGS allows direct use of BETWEEN for logical evaluation on bit-flag types
MySQL and Oracle do not support this feature; BETWEEN must be converted to explicit bitwise expressions (e.g., (col & mask) = mask)

differences.description: Whether data types allow additional specifiers

schema_requirements: The table must include columns using specific data type specifiers (e.g., VARCHAR(50), NUMBER(10,2), DECIMAL(10,2), or other types with length or precision qualifiers)
query_patterns: SELECT CAST(col AS VARCHAR(50)) FROM t;
query_requirements: The query must use data type conversion or definition syntax with parameter qualifiers
Oracle allows exact length/precision specifiers in CAST or functions, while MySQL and PostgreSQL do not support them in certain contexts or behave differently
The test must cover common parameterized types such as VARCHAR, NUMBER, and DECIMAL
data_anti_patterns: Avoid using simple types without parameters (e.g., VARCHAR, INT); otherwise, the DATA_TYPE_SPECIFIERS_ALLOWED difference cannot be demonstrated
key_traps: Oracle supports specifying exact length/precision in CAST (e.g., CAST(x AS VARCHAR2(50)), while MySQL and PG may ignore it or raise an error
When translating across dialects, check whether the target database supports the type specifier; otherwise, adjust the syntax or remove the specifier

differences.description: Whether time zones use WITH TIME ZONE syntax

schema_requirements: The table must include a column of type TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (Oracle-specific syntax; MySQL/PG do not support this type definition)
query_patterns: CREATE TABLE t (ts_col TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE);
query_requirements: The query must use the TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE data type definition
Oracle supports this syntax, while MySQL and PostgreSQL do not support this specific type name (PG uses TIMESTAMPTZ, and MySQL has no native timezone-aware time type)
key_traps: TZ_TO_WITH_TIME_ZONE is an Oracle generator configuration attribute that controls whether a timezone-aware TIMESTAMP type is output
MySQL does not have a TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE type; it typically uses DATETIME or TIMESTAMP (without explicit timezone information)
PostgreSQL uses TIMESTAMPTZ as shorthand, not the TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE string form (although semantically equivalent, the generator behavior differs)

differences.description: Parameter placeholder token

query_requirements: The query must use parameter placeholder syntax
MySQL and Oracle use @ as the parameter prefix (e.g., @id), while PostgreSQL uses $ followed by numbers or letters (e.g., $id or $1)
Note: At the pure SQL execution level, different database drivers handle @ and $ differently; ensure the test environment supports the parameter binding of the corresponding dialect
data_anti_patterns: Avoid using non-standard characters in parameter names, which may cause parsing failures
Avoid using the @ symbol as a parameter prefix in PostgreSQL, as it will cause a syntax error
key_traps: Although both MySQL and Oracle use @, the semantics may differ (in MySQL, @ is a user variable; in Oracle, @ is often used for DBLink or anonymous block parameters)
PostgreSQL's standard parameter is the $N form (positional parameter), while @ in PG is usually used for other purposes (e.g., range operators)
When converting across dialects, adjust the parameter marker format based on the target database; do not simply replace the symbol without considering the context

differences.description: Named placeholder token

query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t WHERE name LIKE %name%
query_requirements: The query must include named placeholder syntax
MySQL and Oracle use a colon (:) as the named placeholder prefix, e.g., :id
PostgreSQL uses a percent sign (%) as the named placeholder prefix, e.g., %name%
During testing, verify the parsing differences of the same placeholder syntax across different dialects
key_traps: MySQL and Oracle use : as the default named placeholder, while PG uses % to avoid conflicts with bind variables
When migrating across dialects, failing to adjust the placeholder marker will cause SQL parsing errors or parameter binding failures
Some ORM frameworks may handle this difference automatically, but native SQL requires explicit adaptation

differences.description: Whether TABLESAMPLE size is the number of rows

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain enough rows of data (recommended at least 1000 rows) so that TABLESAMPLE can sample multiple rows
query_patterns: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t TABLESAMPLE (50 ROWS);
query_requirements: The query must use the TABLESAMPLE clause to specify the sample size
MySQL and Oracle interpret the parameter as the number of rows (ROWS), while PostgreSQL interprets it as a percentage (PERCENT) or requires the explicit PERCENT keyword
In PostgreSQL, without the PERCENT keyword, TABLESAMPLE(10) is treated as 10% rather than 10 rows
data_anti_patterns: Avoid an empty table or one with very few rows (e.g., fewer than 10 rows), otherwise it is impossible to distinguish whether 10 rows or 10% were sampled
key_traps: In MySQL/Oracle, TABLESAMPLE(N) means sampling N rows, while in PostgreSQL, TABLESAMPLE(N) by default means sampling N%

When translating across dialects, if the intention is to sample a fixed number of rows, PostgreSQL must use TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (N PERCENT) and calculate the corresponding percentage, or use other mechanisms to emulate fixed-row sampling
PostgreSQL 14+ supports sampling methods such as BERNOULLI, but the syntax behavior differs from MySQL/Oracle

differences.description: TABLESAMPLE seed keyword

query_requirements: The query must use the TABLESAMPLE clause and specify a seed value
MySQL and Oracle use the SEED keyword, while PostgreSQL uses the REPEATABLE keyword
Both SEED and REPEATABLE syntax must be tested to verify cross-dialect compatibility
key_traps: MySQL and Oracle use SEED as the seed keyword, while PostgreSQL uses REPEATABLE
When translating across dialects, replace SEED with REPEATABLE (PG) or replace REPEATABLE with SEED (MySQL/Oracle)
The seed value must be of an integer type, otherwise syntax errors may occur

differences.description: Query hint separator

query_requirements: The query must use the hint syntax specific to the dialect (e.g., Oracle's /*+ ... */ or MySQL's SQL_NO_CACHE, etc.)
When multiple hints are used, observe the separator differences: Oracle uses spaces to separate them, while PG/MySQL have no built-in concept of a multi-hint separator or rely on different mechanisms
key_traps: Oracle hints must be written inside a comment block and multiple hints are separated by spaces
MySQL hints are usually embedded as keywords in the SELECT statement (e.g., STRAIGHT_JOIN) and do not support multiple hint combinations in the /*+ ... */ format
PostgreSQL does not natively support hint syntax; it must be handled through extensions or at the application layer, making it impossible to directly test separator differences

differences.description: IN/OUT parameter mode separator

query_requirements: This difference belongs to stored procedure/function definition syntax (DDL), not SELECT/DML query statements
MySQL uses IN/OUT keywords followed by spaces or commas to separate parameter modes, while PG uses IN/INOUT/OUT keywords to directly qualify parameters
Oracle uses IN/OUT/IN OUT keywords to qualify parameters, and its parameter list format differs from MySQL/PG
key_traps: INOUT_SEPARATOR is not standard SQL query syntax, but rather metadata configuration or a syntactic convention for stored procedure definitions
MySQL and PostgreSQL handle separators differently in stored procedure parameter declarations, but this is not usually called the INOUT_SEPARATOR attribute
This difference cannot be triggered and tested by pure SELECT statements; it must rely on DDL statements such as CREATE FUNCTION/PROCEDURE

differences.description: Whether the UPDATE statement supports a FROM clause

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain at least two columns (e.g., id and name) for value updates in the UPDATE statement
data_requirements: Related data needs to be inserted into two tables so that rows can be matched via JOIN conditions
The data should contain specific values (such as old names and new names) that can be modified by the UPDATE statement
query_patterns: UPDATE t1 SET name = t2.new_name FROM t2 WHERE t1.id = t2.id;
UPDATE orders o USING customers c SET o.status = 'processed' WHERE o.customer_id = c.id;
query_requirements: The query must use an UPDATE statement that includes a FROM or USING clause to reference other tables
MySQL does not support this syntax; it must be translated into a JOIN form or use a subquery
PostgreSQL and Oracle support FROM/USING clauses and can execute them directly
data_anti_patterns: Avoid single-table operations, otherwise the FROM clause differences for multi-table joins cannot be demonstrated
Avoid data without join keys, as this prevents JOIN conditions from matching
key_traps: MySQL does not support UPDATE ... FROM syntax; you must use JOIN syntax instead
PostgreSQL and Oracle support FROM/USING clauses, but the syntax details differ slightly (Oracle uses USING)
When converting across dialects, note the differences between MySQL's JOIN form and PG/Oracle's FROM/USING form

differences.description: MySQL-specific function: BIT_COUNT

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain an integer-type column (INT, BIGINT, or UNSIGNED) for bitwise operations.
data_requirements: Data should contain non-zero integer values so that BIT_COUNT returns a result greater than 0.
It is recommended to include values with distinct binary patterns (e.g., 1, 3, 7, 255, etc.) to verify counting results for different bit widths.
Optional: include the value 0 as a boundary test.
query_requirements: The query needs to use the BIT_COUNT function to count the number of 1s in the binary representation.
PostgreSQL needs to be translated to BIT_LENGTH(BIT_REVERSE(CAST(int_col AS BIT))) - BIT_LENGTH(BIT_REVERSE(0)) or use the pg_bit_count extension/custom function.
Oracle needs to be translated to REGEXP_COUNT(TO_CHAR(int_col, 'XXXXXXXX'), '1') or simulated with bitwise logic.
data_anti_patterns: Avoid all row data being 0; otherwise, the function's ability to handle non-zero values cannot be demonstrated.
Avoid testing only a single numeric value, as it cannot cover differences in bit width and bit patterns.
key_traps: MySQL's BIT_COUNT supports unsigned integers; negative number behavior may depend on the specific implementation.
PG does not natively support BIT_COUNT; bit operation combinations must be used or the bit_functions extension must be installed.
Oracle has no direct bit-count function; regular expressions or a loop checking bit by bit must be used instead.

differences.description: MySQL-specific function: CONVERT_TZ

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain timezone-related columns (VARCHAR or TEXT type storing timezone names such as 'UTC', 'Asia/Shanghai').
The table needs to contain a DATETIME or TIMESTAMP datetime column.
data_requirements: Data needs to contain datetime values in different timezones to demonstrate the conversion effect.
Data should include at least two different source timezone and target timezone combinations.
Avoid all rows using the same timezone; otherwise, conversion differences cannot be reflected.
query_patterns: SELECT CONVERT_TZ(dt_col, src_tz, dst_tz) FROM t;
query_requirements: The query needs to use the CONVERT_TZ function for timezone conversion.
MySQL supports this function; PG and Oracle do not. It needs to be translated to AT TIME ZONE (PG) or DBTIMEZONE/SESSIONTIMEZONE (Oracle).
data_anti_patterns: Avoid using fixed constant strings as timezone arguments; use column references to test dynamic timezone scenarios.
Avoid testing only conversions within the same timezone; otherwise, the result does not change and the functionality cannot be verified.
key_traps: MySQL's CONVERT_TZ requires the system timezone tables to be configured in order to work properly.
PostgreSQL uses the AT TIME ZONE syntax, while Oracle implements similar functionality using FROM_TZ/CAST or DBTIMEZONE mechanisms.
When converting across dialects, ensure that the target database supports the corresponding timezone name format.

differences.description: MySQL-specific function: CURDATE

query_patterns: SELECT CURDATE() AS today FROM dual;
query_requirements: The query needs to directly call the CURDATE function to obtain the current date.
MySQL returns a DATE type; PG must be translated to CURRENT_DATE or NOW()::date; Oracle must be translated to SYSDATE or CURRENT_DATE.
key_traps: MySQL's CURDATE() is a scalar function that returns a DATE value without timezone.
PostgreSQL does not have a CURDATE function; CURRENT_DATE or CAST(NOW() AS DATE) must be used.
Oracle does not have a CURDATE function; it typically uses SYSDATE (returns DATE+TIME) or TRUNC(SYSDATE) to get the pure date, or uses CURRENT_DATE (affected by the session timezone).

differences.description: MySQL-specific function: CURTIME

query_requirements: Query must call the CURTIME function to get the current time (hour:minute:second or with precision)
PG should be translated to CURRENT_TIME or NOW()::TIME; Oracle should be translated to SYSTIMESTAMP or CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
key_traps: MySQL's CURTIME returns TIME type and can take a precision parameter (CURTIME(p))
PostgreSQL has no CURTIME function; use CURRENT_TIME or NOW() conversion instead
Oracle has no CURTIME function; use SYSTIMESTAMP to extract the time part

differences.description: MySQL-specific function: DATABASE

query_requirements: Query must directly call the DATABASE() function to obtain the current database name
MySQL returns the name of the currently connected database; PG and Oracle do not support this syntax
key_traps: MySQL's DATABASE() is a system function that can be executed without table structures
PostgreSQL has no equivalent function; use current_database() instead
Oracle has no equivalent function; use sys_context('USERENV', 'CURRENT_SCHEMA') or connection information instead

differences.description: MySQL-specific function: DATE_FORMAT

schema_requirements: The table must contain date or time type columns (DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP) for formatting tests
data_requirements: Data should include date values in various formats, including combinations of different years, months, and days
Data should include NULL values to test the function's behavior with empty values
Data should include special dates such as February 29 in leap years, December 31 at year-end, etc., to verify format conversion accuracy
query_requirements: Queries must use the DATE_FORMAT function for date formatting
MySQL uses standard format strings like '%Y-%m-%d'; PG should be translated to TO_CHAR(date_col, 'YYYY-MM-DD'); Oracle should be translated to TO_CHAR(date_col, 'YYYY-MM-DD')
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having all date values exactly identical, as this fails to show output differences among different format strings
Avoid testing only a single format string; cover multiple format combinations such as year-month-day hour:minute:second
key_traps: MySQL's DATE_FORMAT uses percent-prefixed format strings (e.g., %Y); PG and Oracle use template strings enclosed in single quotes (e.g., 'YYYY')
MySQL supports more custom format specifiers; PG/Oracle need mapping to corresponding template syntax, and some complex formats may not be fully equivalent
When converting across dialects, pay attention to timezone issues: MySQL does not distinguish timezones by default, while PG/Oracle may be affected by the session timezone

differences.description: MySQL-specific function: FROM_UNIXTIME

data_requirements: Need to include valid Unix timestamp values (integer type, e.g., 1609459200 represents 2021-01-01 00:00:00)
Data should include timestamps of varying time spans to verify conversion accuracy
query_requirements: Queries must use the FROM_UNIXTIME function to convert Unix timestamps to datetime format
PostgreSQL should be translated to to_timestamp() or epoch::timestamp
Oracle should be translated to TO_DATE('01-JAN-1970','DD-MON-YYYY') + NUMTODSINTERVAL(unix_col, 'SECOND')
data_anti_patterns: Avoid using negative timestamps (which may produce abnormal results in MySQL) unless explicitly testing edge cases
Avoid using NULL values as input; otherwise, it is impossible to distinguish between unsupported function and empty input
key_traps: MySQL's FROM_UNIXTIME returns DATETIME type; PG's to_timestamp returns TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (default UTC timezone)
Oracle has no direct equivalent function; you need to manually calculate the second offset from 1970-01-01
The three databases handle timezones differently: MySQL relies on the server timezone by default, while PG/Oracle handle timezones explicitly

differences.description: MySQL-specific function: ISNULL

schema_requirements: The table must contain at least one numeric column (INT, BIGINT, DECIMAL) or string column (VARCHAR, TEXT) for testing the ISNULL function
data_requirements: Data must include rows with NULL values so that the ISNULL function returns 1 (True)
Data should include rows with non-NULL values so that the ISNULL function returns 0 (False)
For numeric columns, include positive numbers, negative numbers, and zero to cover different scenarios
query_patterns: SELECT ISNULL(col), col FROM t WHERE col IS NULL OR col IS NOT NULL;
query_requirements: Queries must use MySQL's specific ISNULL function
PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support ISNULL; translate to COALESCE/ISNULL alternatives (e.g., CASE WHEN col IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
Oracle can use NVL2 or custom logic to simulate, but the return value type must remain consistent
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having no NULL values in any rows; otherwise, the differential behavior of the ISNULL function cannot be triggered
Avoid using only constant expressions; values must be taken from table columns to reflect dialect differences
key_traps: MySQL's ISNULL returns TINYINT(1), while PG/Oracle have no such function, requiring manual implementation of equivalent logic
When converting across dialects, pay attention to the return value semantics: MySQL returns 1/0; PG/Oracle need to use CASE WHEN to explicitly construct boolean or integer results

differences.description: MySQL-specific function: MAKETIME

query_patterns: SELECT MAKETIME(hour_col, minute_col, second_col) FROM t;
query_requirements: Queries must use the MAKETIME function to construct a TIME value from hour, minute, and second
PG should be translated to MAKE_TIME() or (hour||':'||min||':'||sec)::TIME
Oracle should be translated to TO_DSINTERVAL or string concatenation
key_traps: MySQL's MAKETIME returns TIME type; PG's MAKE_TIME also returns TIME type but with a different function name
Oracle has no direct equivalent function; use string concatenation + TO_DATE to implement

differences.description: MySQL-specific function: SCHEMA

query_requirements: Query must call the MySQL-specific SCHEMA() function to obtain the current database name
PG should be translated to current_database(); Oracle should be translated to sys_context('USERENV', 'CURRENT_SCHEMA') or user
key_traps: SCHEMA() returns the current database name in MySQL, but PG/Oracle do not have this function
MySQL's SCHEMA() differs from PG's schema (mode) concept and cannot be directly mapped to PG's schema name query
In Oracle, the current schema is usually obtained using the USER pseudocolumn or the SYS_CONTEXT function

differences.description: PostgreSQL-specific function: DIV

schema_requirements: The table must contain two numeric columns (e.g., INTEGER, BIGINT, or DECIMAL), serving as the dividend and divisor respectively
data_requirements: Data must include at least two rows, with one row having a divisor of 0 to test safe division behavior
Data should include non-integer division scenarios (e.g., 7 and 2) to verify floor rounding logic
PG should insert integer pairs (7, 2), (-7, 2), (7, -2), (-7, -2) to cover different sign combinations
query_patterns: SELECT dividend DIV divisor FROM t;
query_requirements: Queries must use PostgreSQL's unique DIV operator for integer division
MySQL and Oracle do not support DIV; translate to FLOOR(a/b) or TRUNC(a/b) with type conversion
The result should reflect the floor rounding characteristic (towards negative infinity for negative numbers)
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having all rows be evenly divisible (e.g., 8/2); otherwise, the difference from standard division cannot be observed
Avoid having all divisors non-zero and no negative numbers, as this cannot fully verify sign handling logic
key_traps: PostgreSQL's DIV is an integer division operator that returns BIGINT or INTEGER and rounds towards negative infinity
MySQL and Oracle do not have this operator; use FLOOR() or TRUNC() functions to simulate, noting behavioral differences with negative numbers
When converting across dialects, ensure data type compatibility and avoid implicit type conversion causing precision loss

differences.description: PostgreSQL-specific function: JSONB_OBJECT_AGG

schema_requirements: The table needs to contain two columns: one for the keys of the JSON object (e.g., VARCHAR/TEXT), and another for the values (any type)
data_requirements: The data should contain multiple rows, and the values in the key column should be unique so that the object can be built
The key column values should be non-NULL strings, and the value column may contain NULL, numbers, or text to test handling of different data types
query_patterns: SELECT category, JSONB_OBJECT_AGG(key_col, value_col) FROM t GROUP BY category;
query_requirements: The query must use the JSONB_OBJECT_AGG aggregate function

MySQL and Oracle do not support this function; it must be translated to MySQL's JSON_OBJECTAGG (if version supports it) or manual concatenation, and Oracle requires JSON_OBJECTAGG or an XML conversion approach
data_anti_patterns: Avoid NULL values in the key column, because JSON object keys cannot be NULL
Avoid having the same key value in all rows, otherwise the effect of building an object through aggregation cannot be demonstrated
key_traps: PostgreSQL's JSONB_OBJECT_AGG returns a JSONB type, while MySQL's similar function may return a JSON type
Oracle has no direct JSONB_OBJECT_AGG equivalent; it typically uses JSON_OBJECTAGG, but the return value is CLOB or JSON type, and the syntax details differ slightly

differences.subcategory: Parser functions (supported in PostgreSQL / not in MySQL)
