Only PostgreSQL supports this syntax; MySQL and Oracle need to convert to other forms (e.g., using UNNEST or custom aggregation)
data_anti_patterns: Avoid single-element arrays or empty arrays, as they cannot reflect the differences in VARIADIC's dynamic characteristics
key_traps: VARIADIC is a PostgreSQL-specific syntax used to define variadic functions or handle array expansion
MySQL and Oracle do not support VARIADIC; use UNNEST, recursive CTEs, or custom functions to simulate equivalent functionality

differences.description: Parenthesis-less function mapping: TokenType.CURRENT_CATALOG is supported only in postgres

query_patterns: SELECT CURRENT_CATALOG AS catalog_name FROM dual;
query_requirements: Queries need to directly use the parenthesis-less form of the CURRENT_CATALOG function
MySQL and Oracle do not support this syntax; it needs to be translated to the parenthesized CURRENT_CATALOG() or an equivalent system variable/function
key_traps: PostgreSQL supports calling CURRENT_CATALOG without parentheses, while MySQL and Oracle must add parentheses or do not support this identifier at all

When converting across dialects, change the parenthesis-less form to the parenthesized form CURRENT_CATALOG(), or use each database's corresponding method for obtaining the current catalog name (e.g., MySQL's DATABASE() or Oracle's SYS_CONTEXT)

differences.description: Parenthesis-less function mapping: TokenType.CURRENT_SCHEMA is supported only in postgres

query_requirements: Queries directly use the parenthesis-less form of the CURRENT_SCHEMA keyword
MySQL and Oracle do not support this syntax; translate to DATABASE() and SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'CURRENT_SCHEMA') or schema_name::text respectively
key_traps: PostgreSQL allows CURRENT_SCHEMA to be called as a function without parentheses, while MySQL and Oracle must use parenthesized function forms or specific system variables
When converting across dialects, note: MySQL uses DATABASE(), Oracle uses SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'CURRENT_SCHEMA')

differences.description: Parenthesis-less function mapping: TokenType.LOCALTIME is supported only in mysql, postgres

query_requirements: Queries need to directly use the parenthesis-less LOCALTIME keyword (supported by MySQL/PG)
Oracle does not support LOCALTIME; it needs to be translated to SYSDATE or CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
key_traps: MySQL and PostgreSQL support LOCALTIME as a parenthesis-less function returning the current time
Oracle does not have the LOCALTIME keyword; use SYSDATE, CURRENT_DATE, or CURRENT_TIMESTAMP instead
Note that in MySQL, LOCALTIME() with parentheses is also legal, but the core difference lies in the availability of the parenthesis-less form

differences.description: Parenthesis-less function mapping: TokenType.SESSION_USER is supported only in postgres

query_requirements: Queries need to use the parenthesis-less form of the SESSION_USER function
PostgreSQL supports this syntax, while MySQL and Oracle do not (MySQL/Oracle need to use parenthesized functions or specific system variables instead)
key_traps: In MySQL, SESSION_USER is not a built-in function; use USER() instead
In Oracle, SESSION_USER is a reserved word but is usually accessed as an attribute; the standard SQL syntax may be incompatible, so use SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'SESSION_USER') instead
When converting across dialects, change parenthesis-less calls to the equivalent function calls in the corresponding dialect

differences.description: No-paren function mapping: TokenType.SYSTIMESTAMP is supported only in Oracle

query_requirements: Queries must directly use the SYSTIMESTAMP function to obtain the current system timestamp
Oracle supports calling SYSTIMESTAMP without parentheses, while MySQL and PostgreSQL do not support this syntax
key_traps: In Oracle, SYSTIMESTAMP can omit parentheses, but MySQL and PostgreSQL must use the parenthesized function form or do not support this identifier at all
MySQL requires NOW() or CURRENT_TIMESTAMP instead, while PostgreSQL requires CURRENT_TIMESTAMP or LOCALTIMESTAMP

differences.description: Range operator parser: TokenType.DAMP is supported only in PostgreSQL

query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t WHERE col1 <@> col2;
SELECT col1 <@> col2 as distance FROM t;
query_requirements: Queries must use the PostgreSQL-specific range operator <@> (DAMP) for distance or range comparison

MySQL and Oracle do not support this syntax and need to be translated into equivalent functions (e.g., <@> in PostgreSQL usually has no direct equivalent in MySQL; Oracle requires SDO_GEOM.SDO_DISTANCE)
key_traps: PostgreSQL supports <@> as a range/geometric distance operator, but MySQL and Oracle do not support this symbol at all
When converting across dialects, <@> cannot be retained directly; it must be replaced with database-specific functions or expressions

differences.description: Range operator parser: TokenType.DAT is only supported in postgres

query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t WHERE col BETWEEN start_date AND end_date;
SELECT * FROM t WHERE col DAT '2023-01-01' '2023-12-31';
query_requirements: Query must use PostgreSQL-specific DAT range operator syntax (col DAT 'start' 'end')
MySQL and Oracle do not support the DAT keyword; it needs to be translated to standard BETWEEN ... AND ... or a custom function
key_traps: DAT is a PostgreSQL-specific range operator used as an alternative to BETWEEN syntax
MySQL and Oracle must convert DAT syntax to standard SQL BETWEEN expression for execution

differences.description: Range operator parser: TokenType.MEMBER_OF is only supported in mysql

query_patterns: SELECT col MEMBER OF json_col FROM t;
query_requirements: Query must use MySQL-specific MEMBER OF syntax for set membership testing
PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support this syntax; it needs to be translated to CONTAINS function or IN clause
data_anti_patterns: Avoid executing SQL containing MEMBER OF directly in PG/Oracle; it will raise a syntax error
key_traps: MySQL's MEMBER OF is a feature of the range operator parser; PG/Oracle have no corresponding keyword
PG needs to use @> (array) or jsonb_contains (JSONB) to implement similar logic
Oracle needs to use JSON_VALUE or XMLTable with EXISTS to check membership

differences.description: Range operator parser: TokenType.SOUNDS_LIKE is only supported in mysql

query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t WHERE name1 SOUNDS LIKE name2;
query_requirements: Query must use MySQL-specific SOUNDS LIKE operator for fuzzy matching
PG and Oracle do not support this syntax; it needs to be translated to a phonetic algorithm (e.g., Soundex) or a full-name similarity function
key_traps: SOUNDS LIKE is a MySQL-specific phonetic similarity matching operator; PostgreSQL and Oracle do not natively support it

During cross-dialect conversion, this syntax cannot be preserved directly; an equivalent phonetic algorithm (e.g., Soundex) must be implemented in the target database, or a regular expression can be used to simulate it

differences.description: Statement parser: TokenType.END is only supported in postgres

query_requirements: Query must contain an explicit SQL block terminator (e.g., a DO block or PL/pgSQL block)
PostgreSQL supports using the END keyword as the terminator for code blocks; MySQL and Oracle do not support this syntax structure
key_traps: MySQL and Oracle do not use END as the terminator for anonymous blocks or procedure blocks (Oracle uses END; but requires a complete package structure with DECLARE/IS, and does not support the simple DO $$ ... END $$ syntax)
PostgreSQL DO blocks or PL/pgSQL blocks must end with END, which is a unique syntax feature; cross-dialect conversion requires rewriting it into the corresponding stored procedure or script structure

differences.description: Statement parser: TokenType.SHOW is only supported in mysql

query_requirements: Query must use MySQL-specific SHOW statement syntax
PG and Oracle do not support the SHOW keyword; it needs to be translated to the corresponding system view query (e.g., PG: SELECT datname FROM pg_database;)
key_traps: MySQL's SHOW is a metadata query command; PG and Oracle do not have this syntax structure
When converting across dialects, the SHOW statement must be rewritten as SELECT * FROM system_views; the SHOW keyword cannot be preserved directly

differences.description: Constraint parser: FULLTEXT is only supported in mysql

schema_requirements: Table needs to contain columns of TEXT or VARCHAR type for FULLTEXT index definition
Table structure must support FULLTEXT constraint syntax (only available in MySQL)
query_patterns: CREATE TABLE t (id INT, content TEXT, FULLTEXT(content));
ALTER TABLE t ADD FULLTEXT INDEX ft_idx (content);
query_requirements: Query needs to use the FULLTEXT keyword to define an index or constraint
This syntax is not supported in PostgreSQL and Oracle; it needs to be translated to full-text search specific functionality or removed
key_traps: MySQL allows using the FULLTEXT keyword in CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE to define a full-text index
PostgreSQL uses pg_catalog.tsvector and GIN/GiST indexes to implement similar functionality; the syntax is completely different
Oracle uses packages such as CTXSYS.DRITHSX or text indexes; the FULLTEXT syntax cannot be directly mapped

differences.description: Constraint parser: INDEX is only supported in mysql

schema_requirements: Table needs to contain a regular column (e.g., VARCHAR or INT) for creating an index
query_requirements: Query needs to use a WHERE clause to filter data in order to utilize the index
MySQL supports defining INDEX constraint syntax directly in CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE
PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support using INDEX as a table-level constraint syntax (CONSTRAINT clause); a separate CREATE INDEX statement must be used
data_anti_patterns: Avoid column values being NULL causing the index to not match, which affects test effectiveness
key_traps: MySQL allows using CONSTRAINT ... INDEX syntax in table definitions, while PG/Oracle must use a separate CREATE INDEX statement
When migrating across dialects, MySQL's in-table INDEX constraint definitions must be converted to separate DDL statements

differences.description: Constraint parser: KEY is only supported in mysql

schema_requirements: Table needs to contain one or more columns to define primary key or unique constraints (e.g., INT or VARCHAR type)
query_patterns: CREATE TABLE t (id INT, name VARCHAR(50), UNIQUE KEY (name));
ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT uk_name UNIQUE KEY (name);
query_requirements: Query needs to use DDL statements (CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE) to add a UNIQUE KEY constraint on columns
MySQL allows using the UNIQUE KEY syntax, while PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support this keyword; it needs to be translated to UNIQUE or CONSTRAINT
key_traps: In MySQL, UNIQUE KEY is valid syntax for creating a unique index, but PostgreSQL and Oracle only support the UNIQUE keyword
When converting across dialects, the KEY suffix must be removed from UNIQUE KEY and changed directly to UNIQUE; otherwise PG/Oracle will raise a syntax error

differences.description: Constraint parser: SPATIAL is supported only in MySQL.

schema_requirements: The table must contain spatial data type columns: MySQL uses GEOMETRY/POINT/LINESTRING/POLYGON types; PostgreSQL requires the PostGIS extension and geometry/geography types; Oracle requires the SDO_GEOMETRY type.
The table must include a SPATIAL index constraint: MySQL declares SPATIAL INDEX via the CONSTRAINT keyword in CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE.
data_requirements: Data must include valid spatial geometry object values (e.g., POINT(0,0), POLYGON((...)) in WKT/WKB format).
Data should include at least one non-NULL spatial geometry value to trigger index creation and validation.
query_patterns: CREATE TABLE t (id INT, geom GEOMETRY, SPATIAL INDEX idx_geom (geom));
INSERT INTO t (id, geom) VALUES (1, ST_GeomFromText('POINT(1 1)'));
query_requirements: The query must use the SPATIAL keyword to define the index constraint.
MySQL syntax is CONSTRAINT ... SPATIAL INDEX or INDEX ... SPATIAL.
PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support the SPATIAL keyword as an index modifier; they must use GiST/SP-GIST index syntax or SDO_GEOMETRY-related constraints respectively.
data_anti_patterns: Avoid inserting NULL values into spatial columns; otherwise the validity of the SPATIAL index cannot be verified.
Avoid inserting invalid spatial geometry formats, as all three databases will report errors and the syntax difference cannot be demonstrated.
key_traps: MySQL's SPATIAL is a reserved word at the DML/DCL level, used to declare spatial index attributes.
PostgreSQL must rely on the PostGIS extension and uses the USING GIST syntax instead of the SPATIAL keyword.
Oracle uses the SDO_GEOMETRY type with functions such as MDSYS.SDO_GEOM.RELATE, and has no directly equivalent SPATIAL index declaration syntax.

differences.description: Constraint parser: ZEROFILL is supported only in MySQL.

schema_requirements: The table must contain a numeric column (e.g., INT, BIGINT) with the ZEROFILL attribute defined.
query_patterns: ALTER TABLE t MODIFY col_name INT ZEROFILL;
query_requirements: The query must use DDL statements to create or modify the table structure and explicitly use the ZEROFILL keyword in the column definition.
MySQL supports this syntax; PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support this attribute.
key_traps: ZEROFILL is a MySQL-specific column attribute used to automatically pad leading zeros; PostgreSQL and Oracle do not have this feature.
When converting across dialects, the ZEROFILL attribute must be removed, and formatting functions (e.g., LPAD/PADL) should be used at the query layer to achieve the same effect.

differences.description: ALTER statement parser: MODIFY is supported only in MySQL.

schema_requirements: The table must contain at least one column to test the ALTER TABLE MODIFY COLUMN syntax.
query_patterns: ALTER TABLE t MODIFY COLUMN col_name VARCHAR(100);
query_requirements: The query must use the ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN syntax.
MySQL supports this syntax; PostgreSQL and Oracle do not. It must be converted to ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE.
key_traps: MySQL uses MODIFY COLUMN to change column definitions (type, length, etc.); PostgreSQL/Oracle use ALTER COLUMN ... SET DATA TYPE or a DROP/ADD combination.
When converting across dialects, the MODIFY keyword cannot be kept as-is; it must be rewritten using the target dialect's ALTER syntax.

differences.description: Property parser: FORCE is supported only in Oracle.

schema_requirements: The table must contain a numeric column (e.g., NUMBER or INTEGER) to demonstrate the impact of the FORCE hint on the execution plan.
data_requirements: Data should contain multiple rows so that the optimizer produces different execution paths with and without the FORCE hint.
The data volume should be large enough to trigger a difference between full table scans and index access (e.g., at least 1000 rows).
query_patterns: SELECT /*+ FULL(t) */ * FROM t WHERE id > 100;
SELECT /*+ INDEX(t, idx_id) */ * FROM t WHERE id > 100;
query_requirements: The query must use Oracle-specific /*+ ... */ hint syntax, including FORCE-related directives (e.g., FULL, INDEX).
MySQL and PostgreSQL do not support this syntax; it must be removed or converted to an equivalent hint/plan guidance approach.
data_anti_patterns: Avoid too little data, which causes the optimizer to always choose the same execution plan and makes the FORCE effect invisible.
Avoid cases where all rows satisfy the WHERE condition and no index covers the query; otherwise the FULL/INDEX hint is ineffective.
key_traps: Oracle supports hint syntax such as /*+ FORCE */, but MySQL and PostgreSQL do not support such comment hints at all.
When migrating across dialects, Oracle hints must be removed, and EXPLAIN PLAN or external tools should be used to control the execution plan.

differences.description: Property parser: INPUT is supported only in MySQL and Oracle.

query_requirements: The query must use the INPUT function or syntax structure.
MySQL and Oracle support the INPUT syntax; PostgreSQL does not support it.
key_traps: INPUT is a property parser feature specific to MySQL and Oracle; PostgreSQL does not support it at all.
When migrating across dialects, PostgreSQL must find an alternative or remove this syntax.

differences.description: Property parser: PRIVATE is supported only in Oracle.

schema_requirements: The table must contain a column marked PRIVATE (Oracle-specific syntax, e.g., CREATE TABLE t (col NUMBER) PRIVATE).
Alternatively, the table must contain a private attribute definition (an Oracle-specific DDL extension, not standard SQL).
query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t WHERE col IS NOT NULL;
query_requirements: The query statement itself requires no special syntax; the difference is reflected in the support for the PRIVATE attribute in DDL table creation.
MySQL and PostgreSQL do not support using the PRIVATE keyword in table or column definitions.
Oracle allows adding the PRIVATE attribute to columns in CREATE TABLE statements to restrict access.
key_traps: PRIVATE is an Oracle-specific column-level access control attribute and is not part of standard SQL.
MySQL and PostgreSQL do not support this syntax at all; attempting to execute it will raise a syntax error.
When migrating across dialects, the PRIVATE keyword must be removed or other mechanisms used to simulate access control.

differences.description: SET statement parser: CHARACTER SET is supported only in MySQL.

query_requirements: The query must use SET ... CHARACTER SET syntax to set the character set.
MySQL supports this syntax; PostgreSQL and Oracle do not. It must be translated to ALTER DATABASE/SCHEMA or session-level parameter settings.
key_traps: MySQL's SET CHARACTER SET is a statement-level operation; PostgreSQL and Oracle have no corresponding SET CHARACTER SET syntax.
PostgreSQL uses parameters such as ALTER DATABASE ... SET lc_collate, or specifies encoding at client connection time.
Oracle typically implements this via the NLS_LANG environment variable or ALTER SESSION SET NLS_CHARACTERSET.

differences.description: SET statement parser: CHARSET is supported only in MySQL.

query_requirements: The query must use the SET statement with the CHARSET keyword to set the character set.
MySQL supports the SET CHARSET syntax; PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support this syntax structure.
key_traps: MySQL's SET CHARSET is an independent syntax structure; PostgreSQL and Oracle have no corresponding feature.
In PostgreSQL, similar effects must be achieved indirectly via ALTER DATABASE or session variables (e.g., client_encoding).
In Oracle, NLS_LANG parameters or initialization configurations such as AL32UTF8 must be used.
When converting across dialects, the SET CHARSET statement cannot be translated directly; it must be rewritten into equivalent configuration based on the target database's features.

differences.description: SET statement parser: NAMES supported only in MySQL

query_requirements: Queries must use the SET NAMES statement to specify the character set and collation
This syntax is not supported in PostgreSQL and Oracle and must be translated to the corresponding session setting function or parameter
key_traps: MySQL's SET NAMES is used to set the client connection character set; PG and Oracle have no direct equivalent syntax
PG typically sets the default character set via ALTER DATABASE/USER or uses the client_encoding parameter
Oracle uses the NLS_LANG environment variable or ALTER SESSION SET NLS_LANGUAGE/NLS_TERRITORY for configuration

differences.description: SET statement parser: PERSIST supported only in MySQL

query_requirements: Queries must use the SET PERSIST syntax to set a global variable and persist it to the configuration file
MySQL supports this syntax; PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support this keyword
key_traps: PERSIST is a MySQL-specific SET clause used to write session-level or global variables to my.cnf/my.ini files

PG and Oracle do not support SET PERSIST syntax at all, so an equivalent cannot be implemented (PG requires modifying configuration and restarting, while Oracle requires ALTER SYSTEM SET ... SCOPE=SPFILE)

differences.description: SET statement parser: PERSIST_ONLY supported only in MySQL

query_requirements: Queries must use SET PERSIST_ONLY syntax to set a global variable and persist it across restarts
MySQL supports this syntax; PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support the PERSIST_ONLY keyword
key_traps: MySQL's SET PERSIST_ONLY is used to set persistent global variables; PG/Oracle have no such feature
PG uses ALTER SYSTEM or configuration file changes, while Oracle uses ALTER SYSTEM SCOPE=SPFILE

differences.description: Placeholder parser: TokenType.MOD supported only in PostgreSQL

query_requirements: Queries must use the MOD keyword as the modulo operator
PostgreSQL supports the MOD syntax; MySQL and Oracle do not support this keyword and require translation to % or the MOD() function respectively
key_traps: Neither MySQL nor Oracle supports the MOD keyword as a binary operator; you must use % (MySQL) or MOD(,) function (Oracle) instead
In PostgreSQL, MOD is a valid modulo operator; directly porting it to MySQL/Oracle will cause a syntax error

differences.description: Logical AND operator: TokenType.DAMP supported only in MySQL

query_patterns: SELECT * FROM t WHERE col1 = 1 DAMP col2 = 2;
SELECT col1, col2 FROM t WHERE a = 1 DAMP b = 2 AND c = 3;
query_requirements: Queries must use MySQL's proprietary logical AND operator 'DAMP' (double tilde ~~ or a specific implementation, usually a variant of && or a DAMP token specifically defined in documentation)
Note: The standard MySQL logical AND is AND or &&; if the question specifically refers to 'DAMP' as a non-standard or version-specific syntax, ensure it executes in that environment
PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support this operator and require translation to the standard AND
key_traps: In MySQL, 'DAMP' (usually corresponding to && or a specific dialect marker) is logical AND, but PG/Oracle only support AND
When converting across dialects, 'DAMP' must be replaced with 'AND', otherwise PG/Oracle will report a syntax error
Confirm the specific character representation of 'DAMP' in the test environment (e.g., whether it is && or a special symbol) to avoid confusion

differences.description: Logical XOR operator: TokenType.XOR supported only in MySQL

query_patterns: SELECT col_a, col_b FROM t WHERE (col_a = 1) XOR (col_b = 2);
query_requirements: Queries must use the XOR keyword as a logical operator
MySQL supports XOR; PostgreSQL and Oracle do not support this syntax
key_traps: MySQL's XOR is a binary or multi-ary logical operator that returns a boolean value
PG requires translation to NOT((a AND b) OR (NOT a AND NOT b)) or simulation using CASE WHEN
Oracle requires translation to DECODE(ABS(a-b),1,TRUE,FALSE) or a similar logical expression

differences.description: Logical OR operator: TokenType.DPIPE supported only in MySQL

query_requirements: Queries must use double pipe (||) as the logical OR operator (valid in MySQL), but in PG and Oracle this is a string concatenation operator
MySQL supports using DPIPE (||) for logical OR, while PG and Oracle do not support this usage and require using the OR keyword instead
key_traps: In MySQL, || can be either logical OR or string concatenation (depending on SQL_MODE), while in PG and Oracle || is used only for string concatenation
When converting across dialects, if the original intent is logical OR, MySQL's || must be translated to PG/Oracle's OR

differences.description: Bitwise operator: TokenType.HASH supported only in PostgreSQL

schema_requirements: The table must include integer-type columns (INT, BIGINT, etc.) for bitwise operations
data_requirements: The data should include at least two rows with integer values of different binary patterns to demonstrate the XOR operation effect
It is recommended to include a value of 0 to verify boundary conditions
query_patterns: SELECT id, value1 # value2 AS xor_result FROM numeric_table;
query_requirements: Queries must use the # symbol as the bitwise XOR operator
Operands must be integer-type expressions
Oracle and MySQL do not support # as bitwise XOR and require translation to the BIT_XOR() function or CASE WHEN logic simulation respectively
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having all row data identical, as this prevents demonstrating the bit-flipping characteristic of bitwise XOR
Avoid non-integer data types (such as FLOAT/DECIMAL), which may cause implicit conversion differences or errors
key_traps: In PostgreSQL, # is a valid bitwise XOR operator, while MySQL and Oracle treat it as invalid syntax or a hash character
MySQL has no built-in bitwise XOR aggregate function; typically the XOR keyword (scalar) or a custom implementation is needed
Oracle requires BITAND combined with logical negation or a PL/SQL loop to simulate bitwise XOR behavior

differences.description: Exponent operator: TokenType.CARET is only supported in postgres

data_requirements: Numeric data (e.g., integers or floats) is required for exponentiation
Test data should include positive numbers, negative numbers, and zero to verify results of exponentiation for different bases
query_requirements: The query must use the ^ symbol as the exponentiation operator
MySQL and Oracle do not support the ^ symbol; it must be translated to the POWER() function (MySQL/Oracle) or the POW() function (PG also supports it, but ^ is recommended)
In PG, ^ is native syntax; in MySQL/Oracle, it must be explicitly converted to a function call
data_anti_patterns: Avoid using constant expressions and testing only a single value, as this cannot fully cover differences across the three databases
Avoid cases where the base is 0 and the exponent is negative, as this may cause all dialects to error or return infinity
key_traps: MySQL and Oracle do not support the ^ symbol at all; executing it directly will result in a syntax error
When converting across dialects, the ^ must be replaced with the corresponding POWER(base, exponent) function for the target dialect
Note the argument order of the POWER function: POWER(base, exponent), which is consistent with the ^ operator

differences.description: DDL property PartitionByListProperty has different positions/support across dialects

schema_requirements: The table needs to include a partition structure: MySQL should support LIST partition syntax; PG and Oracle need to use their respective partition syntax (PG uses PARTITION BY LIST, Oracle uses PARTITION BY LIST)
query_patterns: CREATE TABLE t (id INT, category VARCHAR(10)) PARTITION BY LIST(category) (PARTITION p1 VALUES IN ('A'), PARTITION p2 VALUES IN ('B'));
query_requirements: The query needs to use a DDL statement to create a table with LIST partitioning
MySQL places the partition definition after the table column definitions (POST_SCHEMA), while PG/Oracle place the partition definition directly after the table name or as part of a clause
PG and Oracle do not support MySQL's POST_SCHEMA position syntax and must be adjusted to the standard position
key_traps: MySQL allows specifying the partitioning strategy via the PARTITION BY clause after the table column definitions (POST_SCHEMA position)
PG and Oracle must specify the partitioning strategy early in the table definition (e.g., CREATE TABLE t (...) PARTITION BY ...) and cannot append it after column definitions
When converting across dialects, MySQL's POST_SCHEMA syntax should be restructured into the standard position syntax of PG/Oracle

differences.description: DDL property PartitionByRangeProperty has different positions/support across dialects

schema_requirements: The table needs to include columns for range partitioning (e.g., DATE, TIMESTAMP, or NUMBER types)
The MySQL environment must support defining partition properties using POST_SCHEMA syntax
data_requirements: Data should cover multiple range intervals to verify partition boundary handling
Values that fall exactly on partition boundaries should be included (e.g., date boundary points)
query_patterns: CREATE TABLE t (id INT, dt DATE) PARTITION BY RANGE (dt) (PARTITION p1 VALUES LESS THAN ('2023-01-01'));
query_requirements: The query needs to use a DDL statement to define the range partitioning structure
MySQL needs to specify the partition property position via specific syntax after the table definition; PG/Oracle do not support this specific property or use different syntax
data_anti_patterns: Avoid having all data fall within the same partition; otherwise, the partition logic differences cannot be demonstrated
Avoid missing partition boundary values, which would prevent testing boundary behavior
key_traps: MySQL's PartitionByRangeProperty is located at the POST_SCHEMA stage, whereas PG/Oracle have no such concept or implement it completely differently
When converting across dialects, MySQL-specific partition property position must be adjusted to a syntax structure supported by the target dialect

differences.description: DDL property PartitionedByProperty has different positions/support across dialects

schema_requirements: The table needs to include a partition structure: MySQL does not support it; PG needs to use PARTITION BY syntax after the table definition; Oracle needs to specify it after the WITH clause
query_patterns: CREATE TABLE t (id INT) PARTITION BY RANGE (id) (PARTITION p1 VALUES LESS THAN (10));
CREATE TABLE t (id INT) WITH (partition_by='RANGE(id)') PARTITION BY RANGE (id);
query_requirements: The query must be a DDL statement (CREATE TABLE) to test differences in partition property position
MySQL cannot execute any DDL statement containing PartitionedByProperty
PG must insert the PARTITION BY clause after the table column definitions and before constraints
Oracle must specify the partitioning strategy after the WITH clause and before or within PARTITION BY
key_traps: MySQL does not support partition property syntax at all; during DDL conversion, it must be removed or replaced with another mechanism (e.g., sharding)
PG's PARTITION BY must immediately follow the column definitions and cannot be placed in a WITH clause
Oracle's partition properties are typically combined with the WITH clause, and the position is strictly limited to after WITH

differences.description: DDL property TransientProperty has different positions/support across dialects

schema_requirements: The table needs to include column structures that support Oracle's POST_CREATE property (e.g., using VARRAY or nested table types)
The table structure must allow adding properties via ALTER TABLE ADD TRANSIENT PROPERTY after the CREATE TABLE statement
query_patterns: CREATE TABLE t (id INT, data VARRAY VARCHAR(100)); ALTER TABLE t ADD TRANSIENT PROPERTY 'prop_name' = 'value';
query_requirements: The query needs to involve a table structure containing TransientProperty to verify whether the property takes effect
Oracle needs to add the property via ALTER TABLE after DDL execution; MySQL/PG do not support this syntax
data_anti_patterns: Avoid testing simple tables without associated properties, as the differences of TransientProperty cannot be demonstrated
key_traps: MySQL and PostgreSQL do not support the TransientProperty concept at all and will throw an error directly
Oracle only adds the property via ALTER TABLE after the table is created by DDL; it cannot be defined directly in CREATE TABLE
When converting across dialects, Oracle's POST_CREATE logic should be removed or replaced with an equivalent metadata management scheme

differences.description: MySQL time format: %M maps to Python %B

data_requirements: Date data for different months is needed to observe formatting differences in month names
Data should include months that are sensitive to the capitalization of the first letter, such as January and December
query_requirements: The query needs to use a time formatting function to extract the full month name
MySQL uses DATE_FORMAT(col, '%M') to return the full month name (e.g., May)
PG needs to use TO_CHAR(date_col, 'Month') or FM999... format to handle space alignment
Oracle needs to use TO_CHAR(date_col, 'Month'), but the result contains leading/trailing spaces that must be removed with RTRIM
data_anti_patterns: Avoid testing only a single month, as the correctness of month name mapping cannot be verified
Avoid ignoring case sensitivity issues; MySQL %M returns the first letter capitalized, while PG/Oracle Month format may return all uppercase or include spaces
key_traps: MySQL's %M corresponds to Python's %B (full month name), while PG and Oracle's 'Month' format pads with spaces by default
When converting across dialects, note that MySQL outputs 'May' directly, PG outputs 'MAY ' (right-aligned with spaces), and Oracle outputs 'MAY ' (left-aligned with spaces)
